title: Slash commands
plain: A slash command is a word that starts with / and controls Codex, such as /status or /compact. Type / in the message box (the composer) to open the list.
check: What do you type to see the list of commands, and what do you type to narrow the list down to /clear?
rubric: Types / in an empty message box and sees the list of commands
Types a few letters after the slash, such as /cl, to narrow the list
Says the list depends on the place: the CLI lists /clear and /permissions, while the app and IDE extension show a different list
try: In the CLI, type `/` on an empty line, then type `cl`. The list should narrow to /clear. Press Backspace to clear the line; do not press Enter.
pitfall: Wrong belief: every place shows the same commands. Correct: the list depends on where you work; /clear and /permissions are CLI commands in the docs, and the app and IDE extension lists differ.

title: Run a command yourself with !
plain: In the terminal CLI, a line that starts with ! runs a local shell command. It uses the current approval and sandbox settings. Read the command before you press Enter.
check: You type !git status and press Enter. Which settings decide whether that command can run, and where do you read them?
rubric: Names the approval and sandbox settings, and says to read them with /permissions in the CLI
Runs !git status and reads the output in the terminal
Says a command typed by the learner runs for real, so it is read before Enter
try: In the CLI, type `!git status` at an empty prompt and press Enter. Read the output in the terminal.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a command you run with ! skips Codex's rules, so it cannot harm the project. Correct: it uses the current approval and sandbox settings and runs for real, so read it before you press Enter.

title: Side chat with /side
plain: /side opens a side chat that branches from the current chat. Its messages stay out of the main transcript, so you can ask a focused question and return.
check: You ask a side question, then want its answer in the main chat. What do you do, and why is the answer not already there?
rubric: Says the side chat has its own transcript, so the answer is not in the main chat
Copies the needed result back into the main chat with a normal message
Says /side is not available inside another side chat or during review mode
try: Type `/side Check whether this plan has an obvious risk` (use a plan from your chat; /btw does the same). Read the answer, then go back to the main chat.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a side chat is a second window that writes into the main chat for you. Correct: its transcript stays separate, so copy any result you need back with a normal message.

title: Skills
plain: A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file of instructions for one job. Start it with $ and its name, or with /skills. Codex can choose it when your task matches its description.
check: Why does a skill's short description matter more than its instructions when Codex decides whether to use the skill?
rubric: Says Codex first sees each skill's name, description and path, and loads the full SKILL.md only when it chooses the skill
Predicts one request whose words match the description and would make Codex choose the skill
Names the two direct ways to start it: $ with the skill name, or /skills
try: Type `/skills` in the CLI, read two skill names and their descriptions, then close the list without choosing.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a skill runs by itself in the background. Correct: a skill is a folder of instructions, and Codex reads them when it uses the skill. If a new skill does not appear, restart Codex.

title: Subagents
plain: A subagent is a helper agent that Codex starts for a side job, such as a code search. It works on its own and returns a summary. Codex starts one when you ask.
check: You told Codex earlier to use tabs, not spaces. Now you ask it to spawn an explorer agent. What must the request or the agent's instructions say for that rule to hold, and where can you read what the agent did?
rubric: Says the agent gets the task text Codex writes for it and its own custom instructions, so the rule should be written into one of them
Says the subagent inherits the sandbox and approval settings of the main chat
Names /agent as the way to open an agent thread and read what it did
try: Type: Spawn one explorer agent to list the files in this project that contain TODO. Report only the file names. Then type `/agent` and choose its thread.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a subagent knows everything I said in the main chat. Correct: do not assume it remembers a rule. Write the rule into the task you give it, or into its agent file.

title: Hooks
plain: A hook is a command that Codex runs by itself at a set point, such as before a tool runs. Codex runs most hooks only after you review and trust them.
check: A project you received contains .codex/hooks.json, and Codex shows the hook as needing review. What do you do before you trust it, and what happens if the hook changes later?
rubric: Opens /hooks, reads the command the hook runs, and checks what it touches before trusting it
Says a hook runs a command on this computer, so trust only hooks you understand
Says trust is tied to the hook's current definition, so a changed hook needs review again
try: Type `/hooks` in the CLI and read the list of hook sources. This kit adds no hooks, so a new project usually shows none from this kit.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a hook is like a rule in AGENTS.md, only stronger. Correct: AGENTS.md is guidance that Codex reads, while a hook is a command the program runs on your computer.

title: MCP servers
plain: An MCP server gives Codex extra tools, such as access to an issue tracker or a database. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that defines how Codex connects to it.
check: A tutorial says to run `codex mcp add helper --url https://helper.example.net/mcp`. What do you find out before you press Enter, and why?
rubric: Finds out who runs the server and whether that source can be trusted
Says what the server could read or change once connected, such as your files, accounts or data
Says outside content can carry hidden instructions (prompt injection), so the agent may follow text it should not follow
try: Type `/mcp` in the CLI and read the list of servers and tools. Then run `codex mcp list` in a terminal to see the configured servers.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a server from a tutorial is safe because someone listed it. Correct: a listing does not prove the server is safe; check its source and what it can access before you connect it.

title: Communication style
plain: /personality sets a communication style: friendly, pragmatic or none. It changes how Codex talks, not what it is told to do. Rules about the work belong in AGENTS.md.
check: You want Codex to run a formatter after every file edit, without exception. Why is /personality the wrong tool, and what is a better one?
rubric: Says a communication style changes how Codex talks, so it cannot make a step happen every time
Names a hook as the place for a command that must run automatically, and notes that the hook needs trust review first
Says a rule about the work belongs in AGENTS.md, and that the learner should check the result
try: Type `/personality`, pick pragmatic, and ask: What does git status show? Then pick friendly and ask again. Compare the two answers.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a style makes Codex more careful or makes it follow the same steps every time. Correct: a style changes tone and format only, so rules that must always hold go in AGENTS.md or in a check you run.

title: Config files and layers
plain: Codex reads config.toml files in layers. A trusted project's .codex/config.toml beats your user file, and a command-line flag beats both. Type /debug-config to see the layer order.
check: Your project's .codex/config.toml sets one model, and your user config.toml sets another. Which model starts when the project is trusted, and where would you put a one-time override?
rubric: Says the trusted project's .codex/config.toml wins over the user file
Says a one-time override goes on the command line with -c or --config, which beats every file
Says an untrusted project's .codex/ settings are skipped, so the user file applies
try: In the CLI, type `/debug-config` and read the layer order and the policy lines. Change nothing.
pitfall: Wrong belief: my project's .codex/config.toml always applies. Correct: Codex loads it only when you trust the project; in an untrusted project it is skipped, and your user file applies.

title: Models and reasoning effort
plain: A model is the AI that does the work. Reasoning effort sets how much it thinks before it answers. Higher effort is slower and uses more of your usage.
check: You must rename one variable in a small file, and later you chase a bug that appears only sometimes. Which effort would you pick for each job, and what do you give up when you raise it?
rubric: Picks a low or light effort for the rename, because the change is small and clear
Picks a high effort for the intermittent bug, because it needs careful tracing of edge cases
Says higher effort gives slower answers and uses more usage, so raise it only when the result is not good enough
try: Type `/status` and read the model line. Change nothing.
pitfall: Wrong belief: the biggest model at the highest effort is always best. Correct: it is slower and uses more of your usage, so choose the lowest setting that gives a result you can check.

title: Usage limits
plain: Codex is included in ChatGPT plans, and each plan has a usage allowance. /status shows the limits left in the CLI, and /usage shows token activity. Long chats and big tasks use more.
check: A chat has been open all day, and one short question uses a large share of your usage. What explains it, and what do you do before the next unrelated task?
rubric: Says a long chat sends more context with each message, so each reply uses more of the allowance
Runs /status in the CLI to read the remaining limits, or opens the usage dashboard
Names two habits: start a new chat for an unrelated task, and use a smaller model or lower effort for small work
try: In the CLI, type `/status` and read the limit lines. Change nothing.
pitfall: Wrong belief: every message costs the same, so only the number of messages matters. Correct: a long chat carries more context with each message, and big tasks and bigger models use more of the allowance.

title: Writing a good request
plain: A good Codex request names the behavior you want, points to the file or the steps to reproduce it, keeps the constraints, and says how to check the change. Vague requests need more corrections.
check: How would you rewrite 'make the page look better' so Codex knows which page, what better means, and how to check it?
rubric: Names the file or page, for example its file path
Describes the wanted result in words, such as a clearer heading, not only 'better'
Says how to check it, such as a command to run or a screenshot to look at, and what must not change
try: Pick one small change in your project. Write one request with four parts: the file, the wanted result, what must stay the same, and the check. Send it.
pitfall: Wrong belief: Codex knows what I mean, so a short vague request is faster. Correct: a few details save rounds of correction; a vague question is fine only when you want Codex to explore first.

title: Checking Codex's work
plain: Verification means checking Codex's work yourself. Run the tests or commands that check it, and read the diff (the list of changed lines). A summary that says done is not proof.
check: Codex reports 'Done, the login bug is fixed.' Which two things do you do before you believe it, and what does each one prove?
rubric: Runs the project's test command, or asks Codex to run it, and reads the printed result, not only the summary
Opens /diff (CLI) or the review pane (app), or runs /review, and matches each changed file to what was asked
Says tests prove only what they check, and the diff shows what changed, not whether the change works
try: After Codex changes a file in a Git project, type `/diff` in the CLI and read the file names and changed lines.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if Codex says the work is done, it is correct. Correct: a summary is a claim. Only output you can see, such as test results, shows that the change works.
